A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FedLAW research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched across layout changes and renumbering.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix H report original MNIST and CIFAR-10 experiments, including attack comparisons, sensitivity studies, client detection, and communication-round evaluations.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, and Appendix I adds CIFAR-100 results, empirical loss-heterogeneity measurements, and a mimic–misaligned attack study.

M1.justification: The core objective, projection, and Algorithms 1–3 remain unchanged. v2 proposes optional loss-outlier filtering, gradual sparsity-budget reduction when the attacker count is unknown, and periodic weight refreshes. These are limited procedural extensions; their adoption in the retained experiments is not established.

E1.justification: Appendix I.7 adds CIFAR-100 classification under five attack types, extending evaluation beyond the original ten-class datasets. Appendix I.8 adds a distinct MNIST threat scenario combining corrupted gradients with strategically under-reported losses.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the retained benchmark and FedLAW-BSUM comparisons. The new CIFAR-100 table uses the existing baseline set; the mimic study varies attack parameters without introducing another comparison method.

E3.justification: Existing splits, models, training budgets, and Table 1 settings are retained. New protocols measure loss heterogeneity throughout training and evaluate mimic attacks using gradient perturbation magnitude 0.1 and loss-under-reporting parameters 0, 0.1, 0.3, and 1.

E4.justification: Appendix I.6 newly tests the assumption that honest-client loss heterogeneity is small. Appendix I.8 and Figure 9 test whether strategic loss under-reporting prevents malicious-weight suppression. These materially extend robustness analysis beyond the retained sensitivity, BSUM, detection, and communication studies.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-run means and standard deviations. Table 8 and Figure 9 extend this existing practice to new experiments. No increased run count, new confidence-interval procedure, or significance test is reported.

E6.justification: The original accuracy and detection tables retain their values. New Table 8 reports substantial CIFAR-100 findings, including FedLAW accuracy of 37.50±0.15% under label flipping at q=0.6 with 40% attackers, but 1.00±0.00% under LIE at q=0.9 with 40% attackers. New results also quantify loss heterogeneity and delayed malicious-weight suppression under mimic attacks.

T1.justification: Appendix F substantially revises the former Appendix E proof, defining a full-batch auxiliary aggregator with the selected support and deriving mini-batch-to-full-batch bounds. Equation (13) changes the sampling term in C_het from 2ε_S²b_f/(n−b_f) to 2ε_S²n/(n−b_f). New Appendix C adds score inequalities and iterative arguments for strategic attacks.

C1.justification: The introduction newly specifies a cross-silo FL focus with moderately many long-lived clients, narrowing the previously general application framing. The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion otherwise retain the core learning, resilience, convergence, and performance claims.

C2.justification: Appendices B–C expand the mechanism explanation around coherent client subgroups and strategic loss spoofing. Appendix I discusses continued weight adaptation for late attacks and acknowledges degradation on difficult CIFAR-100 settings, especially LIE. These substantially expand interpretations and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 adds practical sparsity-selection and weight-refresh guidance, specifies the mimic attack construction and parameter sweep, and states that CIFAR-100 reuses the CIFAR-10 architecture and protocol. Existing software, GPU descriptions, and the source-code availability statement remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive positioning against existing robust aggregators, BSUM, and prox-linear optimization remain unchanged. The added analyses introduce no new related-work comparison or citation.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are retained. Local edits add explanatory paragraphs and a proof roadmap, remove the introductory paper roadmap, update author/header information, and add acknowledgements. New appendix sections expand the document without extensively rewriting its existing narrative.

P2.justification: The document is reformatted throughout with narrower text and larger body type. Existing figures and tables are substantially rescaled and rearranged; Figure 2 changes colors and caption structure, and tables become more compact. Figure 9 and Table 8 are added, while Tables 3–4 correct their captions from four to five attacks.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the evidence through harder CIFAR-100 evaluation, targeted loss-spoofing tests, and measurements supporting the previously asserted small loss heterogeneity. The revised stochastic derivation also improves transparency. These gains are limited by mimic testing restricted to mild under-reporting and unchanged broad superiority claims despite the failures and baseline exceptions reported in Table 8.
